thread.title: Successful Trade Negotiations With China Could Be Quite Rewarding

author: Michael Chandler
title: Successful Trade Negotiations With China Could Be Quite Rewarding
text:
I cannot think of a more appropriate time than now to drill down into the cornerstone of the trade issues with China. We must have a clear understanding of the trade issues before deciding the merits of investing. The more macro issues, such as currency manipulation and dumping practices, are certainly major concerns and must be addressed in our trade negotiations.
Today, however, we are going to focus on China's theft of intellectual properties. Not only has this become a trade issue but also an issue of national security.
If you remember a few weeks back, the Commerce Department announced it was placing a seven-year ban on China from purchasing much of our technology, specifically semiconductors used in the production of cell phones.
Additionally, on March 12, 2018, Trump blocked the purchase of Qualcomm (NASDAQ: QCOM ) by Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO ) and here is why!
According to Broadcom's most recent annual report , roughly 7 percent of its $17.6 billion in net revenue comes from the United States. The single biggest market for the company is China, which accounted for roughly 54 percent of its net revenue. "Other" markets made up nearly 38 percent.
As a point of comparison, 2 percent of Qualcomm's revenues come from the United States. Some 65 percent of its revenue comes from China, including Hong Kong, according to its most recent annual report .
It appears ZTE ( OTC:ZTCOY ) (the Chinese telecom company) that manufactures cell phones cannot operate without the semiconductors produced by Broadcom and Qualcomm. In fact, after that March 12th announcement, ZTE has nearly shut down most of its production and has cost it thousands of jobs.
China and ZTE violated economic sanctions by selling their phones to both Iran and North Korea . Furthermore, according to the Head of our National Counterintelligence and Security Center Bill Evanina, Chinese Telecom companies have been used to carry out Chinese espionage. It was such a concern, ZTE's products have been pulled from all military installations and are not allowed to be sold in any of the military exchanges.
I find it interesting that within ZTE's corporate structure, there is a Committee of the Chinese Party. Clearly the government has a strong influence in how the company is run.
This company has copied many of the technologies embedded in Apple's (NASDAQ: AAPL ) iPhone. It's been referred to as an iPhone knockoff.
A few weeks back, we mentioned one of the prerequisites to doing business in China was to share your intellectual properties with the government of China. ZTE is a good example of what happens when you are forced to relinquish your IP as a cost of doing business.
It was clearly stated the seven-year ban on sales of technology to China was predicated upon national security and not trade. Nonetheless, the trade impact is substantial.
With 54% of Broadcom's and 65% of Qualcomm's revenues coming from China, they could be significantly harmed if such a ban took effect.
Further trade talks with China promise to be quite interesting, as they continue this week. I suspect more fireworks will be forthcoming.
Trump earlier this week tweeted he now wishes to have some arrangement made to allow the sale of semiconductors to ZTE. The loss of jobs for all three companies would be substantial should the ban be left in place. My guess is there's a significant trade-off coming soon. In fact, it would not surprise me to see some sort of resolution to the IP theft issue.
Here's my rationale! China clearly wants to be the leader of technology and innovation in the world. That was clearly defined back in 2016 when it laid out a new five-year plan laced with significant government subsidies to fund research and development for a multitude of science and technology projects. Its commitment to artificial intelligence is second to none.
The Chinese government is subsidizing patent applications at a tremendous pace, as shown by the World Intellectual Property Organization charts below. I find it interesting it is subsidizing the applications and not the actual patents granted.
China has recently surpassed both the US and Japan in total patents granted as shown above. China is clearly committed to developing new technologies .
It appears to me China is making a concerted effort to develop its own technologies. It could very well be positioning itself for the day in which dependency upon others' intellectual properties is no longer needed.
Hopefully the concern for IP theft will be resolved in this round of trade talks.
There are several misunderstandings regarding the differences between the US and the Chinese economies. For instance, China's GDP is less than 60% of the size of the US economy. China's total GDP is $11.2 trillion compared to the US GDP of almost $20 trillion.
On a per capita basis, China's GDP equates to around $17,000. Here in the United States, that same number is close to $60,000.
China exports approximately 20% of its GDP whereas here in the United States we only export 12%.
There are three things that you can conclude from these statistics: 1) It will be many years before the Chinese economy is anywhere near the size of the United States, 2) the fact the Chinese GDP per capita is so low, you could also conclude, China has a tremendous amount of growing to do within its own borders, and 3) the third conclusion would be if China would domestically grow, it would not have the need to export 20% of the GDP.
China has committed greater than $50 billion a year to its five-year research and development plan, three times that of the US. It has said on many occasions over the past two years that it wanted to grow its economy domestically. China's commitment to infrastructure as well as technology supports that claim.
From an investment standpoint, I suspect there are two areas China will open to free trade. Financials would have to be one of those. The likes of a JPMorgan ( JPM ), which announced today its presence in China, will soon be as large as it is here in the United States. Goldman Sachs ( GS ), Citigroup ( C ), Bank of America ( BAC ) and Morgan Stanley (MS ) will also increase their presence in the Chinese mainland.
With the Chinese government investing in so many startup technology companies by subsidizing their patent applications, there will be a great need for capital to be raised via venture capital, private equity and IPO underwritings. China will be fertile territory for commercial banking.
Infrastructure in China will need substantial investment for many years to come. There are several multinational corporations positioned to take advantage of this opportunity. Caterpillar ( CAT ) would certainly be one that comes to mind.
Then, of course, China will need financing for all these projects which opens yet another opportunity for the banking industry.
It is China's intent to become the Artificial Intelligence (AI) leader of the world. Its version of our Amazon is Alibaba (NYSE: BABA ). Jack Ma, Alibaba's Executive Chairman, has committed significant assets to develop its own AI. This company could be a very rewarding investment over the next 5 to 10 years.
With the trade talks ongoing, there is no one that can absolutely predict their outcome. I believe ultimately, the trade issues between the US and China will be resolved.
Until that happens, Chinese companies, as well as our own multinational corporations, are likely to see extreme levels of volatility. With a fair and open trade accord with China, you would see all the companies mentioned above placing significant investments in the Chinese mainland.
With a long-term outlook, by that I mean 5 to 10 years, China is certainly a country with a promising growth outlook assuming the trade negotiations prove fruitful.
Multinationals are a good way to diversify your portfolio and Asia could be very fertile soil.
